title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
claim: The physiological signal carries both discrete categorical and smooth continuous structure of actions, information that video frames alone only indirectly reveal.
layout: 2 stacked panels, each EMG traces above RGB frames, left-to-right timeline
description: Two stacked time-series panels, each pairing a multichannel EMG plot with a row of egocentric RGB frames. The top panel shows eight rainbow-colored EMG channels (numbered 1 to 8, red to pink) across six gesture segments labeled Fist, Point, Flat, Fist, Point, Flat. Grey rectangles mark each gesture window. Below the traces, fisheye frames show a hand on a balcony wearing a wristband, separated by ellipses. The bottom panel shows a pick-and-lift sequence labeled Rest, Pregrasp, Grasp, Lift, Hold. Soft gradient grey bands mark gradual transitions between phases. EMG amplitude builds from quiet at rest to a sharp peak at lift, then stays elevated during hold. Kitchen-scene frames below show a hand reaching for a potted plant and lifting it. Row labels (EMG Channels, RGB Frames) sit on the left. The eye goes first to the dense colorful traces.
caption: EMG captures both categorical and continuous structure of hand actions. (Top) For three discrete hand configurations repeated twice—fist, point, and flat—each pose produces a distinct and reproducible EMG signature: fist is marked by a suppressed purple channel (#7) with respect to flat and a pronounced red channel (#1) with respect to point; point exhibits lower overall amplitude, with less purple than flat and less red than fist; flat is distinguished by pronounced purple and red activation. Sharp grey rectangles reflect the boundaries between hand gestures and rest states. (Bottom) A pick-and-lift sequence combines gradual and abrupt transitions: the hand moves smoothly from rest through pregrasp into grasp, changes sharply as force is applied at lift, then settles—non-instantaneously—into a steady hold. The EMG mirrors this structure, with channels quiet at rest, building subtly through pregrasp and grasp, peaking sharply as the lift begins, and stabilizing during hold.
abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
